newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty creeps lower, looks to NBP for help.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty creeps lower, looks to NBP for help.

text.p: The Polish zloty crept lower against its currency basket on Thursday as news of another wave of heavy rains and floods expected this weekened did little to stop fleeing foreign portfolio investors, dealers said.

They said the zloty's decline was limited because banks were wary of a National Bank of Poland's (NBP) intervention to lift the zloty after the finance ministry and the IMF both signalled that the local currency's slide has been excessive.
"The zloty is being pushed down by exiting foreigners and the market is waiting for the NBP to intervene and potentially pull the zloty back up," said Tomasz Wolosz, dealer at BRE SA.
The zloty closed at -3.78/-4.23 percent from the trading band centre, against Wednesday's -2.73/-4.24 percent.
It closed at 3.4900/5100 to the dollar against 3.4550/050 on Wedneday and at 1.9500/50 to the mark against 1.9285/575.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said the recent zloty selling trend should be reversed, but the market remained bearish on the local curency, which lost five percent over the last week, and kept the local unit gradually headed downward on Thursday.
The money market relaxed slightly after several days of nearly no liquidity and rates slipped from levels nearly reaching the 25 percent lombard rate, dealers said.
Overnight rates closed at 22.80/23.20 percent, down from opening's 23.65/23.85 percent and tomorrow/next at 22.90/23.30 percent from 23.70/23.90.

Earlier today in a special session on flood relief funding, the parliament passed an amendment to the 1997 budget which increased by 2.5 billion zlotys the amount of treasuries the government can sell to the NBP.

"This means the NBP will have to sterilise large amounts of cash, pulling up market rates, and it creates some room for an official interest rate rise," said Robert Gluch, dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.
Economists said the central bank could opt for an official interest rates rise because an inflow of hot foreign capital was not expected amid bearish zloty sentiment.
